title: Point of care ultrasound and echocardiography

steps.tx: The **BLUE protocol** uses lung sliding and artefacts when breathlessness is acute. Bilateral **A lines** with sliding suggest bronchospasm or embolism. Bilateral anterior **B lines** suggest pulmonary oedema. The pattern sorts a likely cause at the bedside. It does not replace the examination, and it does not by itself choose the ventilator settings.

vis.caption: Key lung ultrasound findings for acute respiratory failure

steps.tx: **Lung sliding** rules out **pneumothorax** at that interspace only. Absent sliding with A lines is not enough, because a main bronchus plug can look the same. A **lung point**, where sliding reappears beside absent sliding, confirms pneumothorax. No lung point does not exclude a large pneumothorax. Treat a crashing patient on clinical signs.

steps.tx: The **RUSH** exam looks at the pump, the tank, and the pipes in shock. The pump is ventricular squeeze and the pericardium. The tank is the **inferior vena cava** and free fluid in the abdomen. The pipes are the aorta and the femoral veins. A single view is not a complete RUSH exam.

steps.tx: In a spontaneously breathing patient, **inferior vena cava collapse** of more than 50% with a sniff suggests low right atrial pressure. That finding does not by itself prove a fluid bolus will raise cardiac output. In fully controlled ventilation, **distensibility** above 18% is the cutoff often used to predict fluid responsiveness. Do not mix the two cutoffs.

steps.tx: **Tamponade** is a clinical and Doppler diagnosis, not a fluid measurement. **Right atrial systolic collapse**, right ventricular diastolic collapse, and a plethoric inferior vena cava support it. Electrical alternans is a late electrocardiogram clue. The treatment of obstructive shock from tamponade is drainage. Fluid alone does not fix a pressurised pericardium.

steps.tx: Stroke volume is left ventricular outflow **velocity time integral** times the cross sectional area. An integral around 18 to 22 cm is typical in an adult. A rise of at least 10% after a passive leg raise predicts fluid responsiveness better than a single static number. A low integral has many causes, including obstruction and a failing left ventricle.

steps.tx: The extended **FAST** exam adds both pleural spaces to the perihepatic, perisplenic, pelvic, and pericardial views. A free fluid stripe in a shocked trauma patient is a reason to go to haemorrhage control. It is not a reason to wait for a CT while the blood pressure is falling. A negative FAST does not exclude retroperitoneal bleeding.

steps.tx: Point of care ultrasound answers a **focused question** and is repeated when the question changes. A saved clip is more useful than a memory of a grey image. The same patient can have oedema on the lung views and tamponade on the heart views, so one normal window does not clear the others. Document what you saw and what you did not look at.
